tagline: A creek gorge, coal ovens and a climb to high land
intro: Old Route 7 follows WV 7 east from Morgantown toward Maryland, winding beside Deckers Creek before crossing the Cheat River and climbing Briery Mountain. Limestone outcrops, rhododendron and laurel line the creek's narrow gorge. The Federal Highway Administration presents the byway as a 43-mile drive and suggests allowing an hour and a half. Along that creek section, gently flowing water becomes a tumbling torrent through the gorge; after the Cheat crossing, the mountain climb opens views from the road.

The corridor's industrial history takes physical form near Masontown, where a coke works began production in 1907 after the railroad arrived. Bethlehem Steel acquired it in 1918 and moved production to more efficient Baltimore facilities in 1920. Nearby Arthurdale began in 1933 as a federal experiment offering homes and opportunities to unemployed local miners and farmers. Eleanor Roosevelt helped secure government approval and pressed for insulation and indoor plumbing in the houses.

Driving east, begin at the Monongahela River in Morgantown and follow the creek toward Masontown. The water calms as the route passes near Arthurdale. Continue through Kingwood to the Cheat crossing, then climb Briery Mountain to 2,735 feet. Terra Alta occupies the mountaintop before the route reaches the Maryland line.

moments.title: Masontown
moments.text: A row of 140 stone-and-brick coke ovens follows the hillside above Deckers Creek, about half a mile southwest of Masontown. Coal entered through openings at the tops of the domes; finished coke came out through arches in their sides. Electric hoppers once moved along tracks above the ovens, while railroad cars received coke below. Those tracks are gone, along with the office, storage and maintenance buildings. Production began in 1907 after the railroad reached Masontown. Bethlehem Steel acquired the works in 1918, then shifted production to Baltimore in 1920. Intermittent use followed before permanent closure in the 1980s.

moments.title: Arthurdale
moments.text: Arthurdale put a New Deal proposal into houses: unemployed miners and farmers would have homes and land to grow food. Construction began in late 1933, with Eleanor Roosevelt pressing for indoor plumbing and insulation and choosing the refrigerators herself. The promise had exclusions. Black and Jewish miners were excluded; Roosevelt deferred to local sponsors and recommended separate communities for the excluded miners. Most families could not grow enough food to support themselves. Property passed into private ownership in 1941, though federal subsidies and supervision continued until 1947. More than 100 original buildings survive, alongside a New Deal museum.

moments.title: Terra Alta
moments.text: Terra Alta means “high land” in Latin, a name that fits the town at the top of Briery Mountain. WV 7 climbs to 2,735 feet after crossing the Cheat River. The town began in the 1850s under another name, Portland. An 1876 Baltimore and Ohio Railroad map identifies its railroad stop as Cranberry Station, adding a third name to the same town's transport history. The James S. Lakin House and Terra Alta Bank are both on the National Register of Historic Places. Beyond Terra Alta, the byway continues to the Maryland state line.
